Preventing Scientific Misconduct
  • Source: American Journal of Public Health, Vol. 88, No. 1 (January 1998)
  • Topic: Framework for preventing scientific misconduct using public health models
  • Author(s): Douglas L. Weed, MD, PhD
Definition of Scientific Misconduct
  • Two federal definitions emerged in early 1990s: National Science Foundation and Department of Health and Human Services
  • Both define misconduct as: fabrication, falsification, plagiarism, or serious deviation from accepted practices in proposing, conducting, or reporting research
  • Debate over inclusion of "other serious deviation" phrase
  • Proponents --> allows scientific communities to define ethical conduct for their branches of science
  • Opponents --> term too broad
  • No known cases where innovative science was wrongly sanctioned despite this concern
Federal Commission's Expanded Definition (1995)
  • Research misconduct = serious violation of fundamental principle that scientists must be truthful and fair
  • Unethical conduct includes:
  • Misappropriation (plagiarism or breaches of confidentiality)
  • Interference
  • Misrepresentation (falsification or fabrication)
  • Obstruction of investigations
  • Noncompliance with research regulations
Controversy Over Broad Definitions
  • Some believe broad definitions --> ↑ investigations because includes any behavior judged untruthful or unfair
  • Others argue misconduct should be very broadly defined to include behaviors beyond fabrication, falsification, and plagiarism
Deceptive Scientific Practices (Less Serious Misconduct)
  • Misrepresentation of research results = most commonly cited deceptive practice
  • Failure to explain weaknesses in data
  • Selective reporting of results
  • Failure to publish studies with negative results
  • Reporting as "negative" a study that had low power
Irresponsible Practices Also Designated Misconduct
  • Honorary authorship
  • Wasteful (repetitive) publication
Continuum of Scientific Conduct
End Description
One extreme Serious misconduct (fabrication, falsification)
Middle Deceptive reporting practices
Middle-adjacent "Sloppiness"
Other extreme Appropriate conduct including unintentional error
Error vs. Misconduct
  • Science progresses because error exists in measurement and interpretation
  • Errors are unintentional
  • Misconduct involves intentional misrepresentation or misappropriation
Estimating Prevalence of Scientific Misconduct
  • Published opinions are polarized:
  • Some believe misconduct is rare
  • Others believe it is rampant
Prevalence Estimates
  • Lancet editorial: fraud alone = 0.1%–0.4% of research studies
  • No source provided for this estimate
Three Types of Empirical Studies
Type 1: Written Records Examination
  • Examined published papers and employment applications for accuracy
  • Sekas & Hutson findings:
  • 30% of gastroenterology fellowship applicants who claimed prior publications fabricated either the article or journal cited
  • Slightly higher percentage misrepresented research experience
  • Gurudevan & Mower findings:
  • Lower but significant rates of misrepresentation in emergency medicine residency applications
  • Misrepresentation rate ↑ with number of citations
Type 2: Questionnaire Surveys
  • Assessed respondents' knowledge of misconduct among colleagues
  • Swazey et al. findings:
  • 9% of 2600 students and faculty had "direct knowledge" of faculty who plagiarized
  • When definition expanded to include honorary authorship, sexual harassment, misuse of research funds, safety violations:
  • 44% of students and 50% of faculty had observed or had direct evidence
Type 3: Routine Data Auditing
  • Shapiro & Charrow found serious deficiencies in investigational drug programs:
  • 12% in 1985 --> 7% in 1988
  • Nearly 2000 investigators examined
  • Misconduct also tracked through Office of Research Integrity (US Public Health Service) records
Impact of Misconduct
  • A single well-publicized case --> considerabledamage to:
  • Institutions
  • Scientists' reputations
  • Public's perception of science
  • Example: recent case of fabrication in large government-sponsored cancer treatment trial
Key Principle
  • Scientific misconduct must not be ignored or trivialized regardless of its prevalence
Framework for Prevention: Overview
  • Preventing scientific misconduct = widely recognized goal
  • Misconduct should be considered a professional affliction
  • Amenable to both primary and secondary prevention
Primary Prevention of Scientific Misconduct
Definition
  • Identifying and removing causes of events
  • Identifying factors whose presence (not absence) actively reduces occurrence
External Causes of Misconduct
  • Publication pressure --> most frequently cited cause
  • Leads to "publish or perish" culture
  • Competition among scientists
  • Large scale of science
  • Reduces opportunities for effective mentoring
  • Fewer senior scientists to monitor behavior
  • Mentors setting bad examples
Internal Causes of Misconduct
  • Personal financial gain
  • Ego or vanity ("fame and fortune viper")
  • Psychiatric illness
  • "Remove" via effective psychiatric treatment --> some misconduct could be prevented
  • Mentally impaired but employable scientists specifically targeted
Important Caveat on Causes
  • Reducing or eliminating publication pressure and competition might also reduce what makes science rigorous and productive
  • May be a matter of degree
Proposed Interventions for External Causes
Publication Pressure Solutions
  • Emphasize quality over quantity in academic appointments and promotions
  • Eliminate honorary authorship
Large Scale of Science Solutions
  • Increase opportunities for mentoring by ↑ ratio of senior to junior scientists
  • Assumption: resources are available
Paradox Identified
  • Providing more mentors ≠ providing good mentors
  • Bad mentoring itself is a proposed external cause of misconduct
Ethics Education Approaches
Codes of Responsible Conduct
  • Rules or guidelines for appropriate scientific and professional practice
  • Often-cited approach to teaching ethics within context of misconduct
Fundamental Problems with Rules-Based Ethics Teaching
  • Thousands of decisions not covered by rules in any professional scientific practice
  • Question: what kind of individual follows rules in the first place?
  • Ethics (like science) has theories and methodologies beyond rules
  • These help interpret rules and guide practice where rules are missing
Virtue Ethics as Alternative Foundation
  • Theory of virtue ethics or character ethics
  • May be necessary for any account of scientific misconduct ethics
Key Virtues for Science
Virtue Application to Scientific Conduct
Honesty Develop habitually rather than dishonesty
Self-effacement Put interests of profession and society (especially research subjects) before personal interests
Excellence Habitually exhibit excellence rather than sloppiness
Why These Virtues Matter
  • Internal good of science = truth
  • Science is a search for the "really real" of the world
  • Fabrication, falsification, misappropriation, misrepresentation = direct affronts to this search
Developing Virtue Ethics in Scientists
  • Can be taught from literature and case studies
  • Most efficacious approach: learn by example
  • Observe, emulate, reflect upon virtuous behavior of respected mentor
  • Mentors must:
  • Possess requisite virtues
  • Habitually display them in everyday scientific practice
Remedial Ethics Education
  • Some senior scientists may need remedial ethics education (based on recent misconduct cases)
  • No guarantee that learning virtuous scientific life will lead to right actions or motivations
Potential Impact of Virtue Ethics Training
  • If virtues of honesty, self-effacement, and excellence could be instilled during training:
  • Three causes of misconduct might potentially be modified:

1. Mentors setting bad examples

2. Personal financial gain

3. Ego or vanity

Problems with Primary Prevention Framework
Problem 1: Weak Evidentiary Basis
  • Proposed causes of scientific misconduct are based on expert opinion only
  • This evidence category is "almost always fraught with opposing views"
  • Example of conflicting expert opinions:
  • Pellegrino states: "fraud is not the product of deranged or unhinged minds"
  • Royal College of Physicians states: "a... cause of scientific misconduct is psychiatric illness"
  • Both with note that "[there are] no data on this issue"
Problem 2: Attribution Questions
  • How much misconduct can be attributed to these causes?
  • How much remains unexplained?
Problem 3: Determining Intervention Effectiveness
  • How to determine if suggested preventive interventions are effective in reducing misconduct?
  • These questions are closely related in public health model
The Public Health Model Applied
  • Attribution requires a decision regarding causality
  • To attribute cases of misconduct to a particular factor = assume that factor is (or can reasonably be judged to be) causal
  • Answering intervention question may help answer cause question
The Causal Test
  • One of the best tests of a causal hypothesis = remove the cause and observe the preventive intervention effect
  • But: surveillance systems must be in place to track misconduct before and after intervention
Evidence Gap
  • Primary preventive interventions in public health are rarely attempted without reasonable body of evidence supporting underlying causal hypothesis
  • Evidence for proposed causes of scientific misconduct = extraordinarily weak
Need for Formal Research on Misconduct Determinants
  • May be time to formally study determinants of scientific misconduct
  • Will require behavioral and social science methodologies
  • Misconduct represents mostly deliberate and conscious acts by perpetrators
  • Causes are more "historical" than "natural" (Collingwood's categorization)
Challenges in Studying Causes
  • Most commonly cited causes (publication pressure, competition) are like universal environmental factors
  • Nearly everyone in science is exposed
  • Causes are not independent of one another
Proposed Research Methods
  • Surveys of professional groups regarding knowledge, attitudes, and beliefs about misconduct in science
  • Better empirical estimates of prevalence and incidence rates
  • Case-control studies where case subjects = those who have committed misconduct
Expected Methodological Problems
  • Case ascertainment difficulties
  • Recall bias
  • Other forms of information bias
  • Confounding
Secondary Prevention of Scientific Misconduct
Definition in Public Health Model
  • Early detection of disease events coupled with effective treatment
  • For misconduct: early detection = ↑ opportunities for discovering instances
Early Detection Strategies
Auditing
  • Most obvious strategy for finding misconduct
  • Periodic review of scientific records, publications, and workloads
Increased Mentoring Ratio
  • ↑ ratio of senior to junior scientists = form of secondary prevention
  • One role of mentor = monitor behavior of junior colleagues
Institutional Responsibility Requirements
  • Early detection approaches require concomitant acceptance of responsibility by:
  • Institutions and their leaders
  • Working scientists (especially)
  • Responsibility = do something about scientific misconduct
Most Difficult Responsibility
  • Reporting misconduct perpetrated by colleagues
  • Many authors recommend protection for whistle-blowers
Investigative Procedures and Due Process
Institutionalization of Procedures
  • Often recommended for handling cases of alleged misconduct
Due Process Requirements
  • Essential to institutional review process (moral and legal grounds)
  • Same principle as informed consent in medical research
Purpose of Investigative Procedures
  • Provide structure for judging facts of cases
  • Ensure appropriate penalties ("treatment") are meted out
Effects on Accused Scientists
  • Misconduct investigations entail "trouble and disgrace"
  • Effects apply to both:
  • Those found guilty
  • Those wrongly accused
Sanctions and Consequences
Federal Funding Ineligibility
  • Regular reports from Office of Research Integrity detail this sanction
  • Those convicted of misconduct = ineligible for federal funding
  • Serious punishment for scientists whose livelihood depends on outside funds
Publishing Sanctions
  • At least one journal has published sanctions for inappropriate acts
  • Example: fabrication brings penalty of "two years to life"
  • During this time, author may not submit manuscript for consideration
Monetary Awards
  • Recent legal case: theft of intellectual property
  • Plaintiff awarded just over $3 million
Problems with Secondary Prevention Framework
Problem 1: Surveillance Paradox
  • Any form of increased surveillance (formal auditing or informal encouraging to report) --> ↑ number of misconduct cases detected
  • However: this increase may represent not a true change in underlying incidence
  • Rather: apparent change due solely to more intense surveillance
  • Well-known phenomenon in programs designed for early disease detection
The Misinterpretation Risk
  • ↑ numbers of misconduct cases from increased surveillance could be misconstrued by:
  • Commentators
  • Press
  • Legislators
  • Others
  • Could be seen as indicative of a larger problem than truly exists
Problem 2: Effectiveness of Sanctions
  • Extent to which sanctions prevent further incidents = unexplored empirical question
  • Potential preventive effects from:
  • Institutional investigational procedures
  • Monetary and publishing disincentives
  • Other strategies (e.g., firing guilty party)
  • May engender second thoughts about committing misconduct among:
  • Would-be repeat offenders
  • Would-be first offenders
Tertiary Prevention (Summary Section)
Definition
  • Rehabilitation and long-term care aspects
  • Applied to scientific misconduct: those who commit misconduct may require rehabilitation before returning to scientific practice
Author's Conclusion
  • More complete analysis will likely lead (as with primary and secondary prevention) to questions based on relatively little empirical information
Key Questions That Emerged
  • What are the true causes of misconduct?
  • How much can be attributed to various factors?
  • Which interventions actually work?
Author's Perspective on Difficulty
  • Answers will be difficult to obtain, especially if precise scientific methodologies are employed
  • But: "we are scientists, and solving difficult empirical problems is what we do best"
Essential Question
  • Less methodological than motivational
  • Are scientists willing to study their own conduct as scientists?
Author's Recommendations (Not Delayed by Research)
Immediate Actions
  • Do not postpone interventions until etiology fully understood
  • Including underlying biological, behavioral, and social mechanisms
Specific Recommendations
  • Implement fair investigative procedures now
  • Expand discussion of ethics in conduct of science and medicine (perhaps on faith)
  • Those who act as mentors --> conduct themselves virtuously
Final Imperative
  • For the sake of those trained and especially for those whose lives are improved by scientific results:
  • Must exhibit excellence
  • Must exhibit self-effacement
  • Must exhibit, above all, an unwavering commitment to the truth
